newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Employment plans split S.African labour, business.
newsitem.headline: Employment plans split S.African labour, business.

text.p: Fresh battle lines are being drawn between South African business and labour over employment legislation which industry fears will increase its costs but which unions argue is vital to protect workers.
The labour federation Cosatu is mobilising for a one-day strike on May 12 to ensure key elements of the Employment Standards Bill are not watered down.

Employers object strongly to certain proposals in the bill and to separate plans for a 1.5 percent training levy which Labour minister Tito Mboweni wants applied across the board to tackle South Africa's chronic skills shortage.

The South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) argues that the costly training levy, coupled with the standards bill and the fallout of a national strike, could jeopardise the job-creating potential of the economy in 1997.

"The need to address labour market flexibility is crucial to creating new jobs in an environment where the stripping of protective barriers has already contributed to labour shedding," Sacob said on Tuesday.
The final version of Employment Standards Bill has not yet been published but business is concerned over proposals for a reduction in the maximum working week.

The main components of the bill -- expected to be put before cabinet towards the end of April -- are likely to include a reduction in maximum working hours to 45 from 46 and subsequently to 40 hours over five years.

Most of industry is currently working on a maximum week of 46 hours, although exceptions are security guards (currently at 60 hours) and workers in the mining, farming and parts of the construction industry (48 hours).

Other proposals expected include an increase in annual paid leave from two to three weeks a year and maternity leave from three months to four months, as well as raising the overtime premium from time and a third to time and a half. Two major concerns for employers are the increased unit labour costs and the limited labour market flexibility implied by the bill.

Says Business South Africa negotiator Adrian du Plessis: "In the view of business, the bill does not find the right balance and runs the risk of advancing labour standards at the expense of economic efficiency."

Labour, business and government have been in talks in the labour market chamber of the National Economic Development and Labour council about the new employment standards law since early last year but have so far failed to reach agreement.

Sacob labour affairs director Gerrie Bezuidenhout says business is concerned about the increased costs involved in the bill which will only be aggravated by the planned 1.5 percent training levy on payrolls.
"The levy will actually be an additional tax on business," he said.
In the current economic climate business could ill afford added costs.
"The hope is that government will bear in mind that to address the unemployment problem and create jobs, business cannot be burdened with a lot of additional costs," Bezuidenhout said.
